_comment: LINEDOWN — manifest for the beat-5 marking fixture set. Load this instead of globbing.
Each entry points at a .json (structured), a .txt sidecar (flat, generated from the .json),
and an .svg label image where one exists.
TEXT-FIRST BY DESIGN: `data/markings/marking-strings.txt` carries every discriminator in the
whole set as flat tagged lines. If Moss image embedding is unavailable (MILESTONES.md risk
register, row M1), beat 5 runs unchanged off that file using string, regex, range and date
comparisons. The images are the nicer visual, never the mechanism.
GENERATED FILES: every .txt is generated from its sibling .json. Edit the .json. The two
generator scripts used are throwaway and live outside the repo; regeneration is a 20-line
script and the .txt files are committed, so nothing depends on them existing.
ILLUSTRATIVE: all marking strings, lot codes, serial ranges, glyph-profile names and pattern
weights are fabricated for the demo. 'Pacific Rim Components Ltd.' and lot PRC-24817 are
invented. 'Reference cluster A' is an invented construct modelled on the shape of industry
counterfeit advisories. None of this is real anti-counterfeit reference data.
MODULE vs DIE: the entire set is module-level — adhesive labels and DRAM package top markings
on assembled 288-pin RDIMMs, plus SPD contents read over I2C. Nothing was decapsulated and no
claim is made about which DRAM die is inside any module. The defensible claim is narrower and
stronger: the module is not the part it says it is, so none of our qualification data applies.
beatLabel: Broker offer → photograph DIMM → Moss matches counterfeit marking

eventRefs.toolCall: e035 — moss, 'Matching module top-marking, FBGA code and lot/date code against reference lots'
eventRefs.toolResult: e036 — moss.matches, latencyMs 0.2, three scored references
eventRefs.counterfeitFlagged: e037 — counterfeit.flagged, score 0.93, imageA vs imageB side by side

fixtures.role: THE BASELINE — imageB in e037. The part the suspect lot claims to be.
The pattern the 0.93 score is measured against. Answers 'similar to what?'.
The approved winner, and the low-similarity control (0.18) that proves the matcher discriminates.
Completeness. The schedule-rejected candidate's clean record — rejected on lead time, not quality.

similarityMatrix._comment: The three scores e036 reports. They matter together: high against the remarked pattern, low against the part it claims to be, lower still against an unrelated genuine part. A matcher that flagged everything would prove nothing.
similarityMatrix.latencyNote: MOSS's MEASURED local-backend query time (status/moss.md), not an invented figure. Excludes parseMs — never add parseMs to latencyMs. Stage wording is 'on-device retrieval', NOT 'fully offline': index creation is a cloud operation and only the query is local. The honest version of the confidentiality point is that the QUERY never leaves the laptop.

photoSwapProcedure._comment: The user is photographing a real DIMM — one genuine, one with an altered label. These are an UPGRADE, not a dependency: the schematic SVGs are a legitimate shipping artifact and may project more legibly than a phone photo under venue lighting.
photoSwapProcedure.rule: The event log (data/mock-events.json e036/e037) references these exact paths and MUST NOT be edited to accept a photo.
photoSwapProcedure.viewBox: 0 0 440 210 (~2.1:1) — fixed, so a 4:3 phone photo letterboxes predictably instead of reflowing the beat-5 layout
photoSwapProcedure.preferredMethod: Overwrite the .svg in place with an <svg> wrapper containing an <image> element pointing at the photo, or replace the file with the photo and keep the filename. Zero code change.
photoSwapProcedure.alternateMethod: Drop a same-stem .png beside the .svg and have the UI asset resolver prefer .png when present. One line in the UI, no data change.
photoSwapProcedure.deadline: 16:30 feature freeze. If the photos are not in by then, ship the SVGs — they are complete and correct as-is.
